title: The golden mouth
hook: John Chrysostom: if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rome falls, and your line was two cities, two loves. Which city did your hours build? Day seven hundred eighty-two.

Silk in the church. Gold cups for the wine. A preacher stands in a church full of beautiful things, and he points past all of it, to the door, and to the man sitting outside it, asking for bread. The preacher is John, a priest of Antioch who later became bishop of Constantinople. People came to call him Chrysostom, which means golden mouth. Today: what the golden mouth said about that door.

The sermon is one of his homilies on Matthew's Gospel. He's speaking about the bread and the cup, the body of Christ at the altar, and he speaks of it with deep reverence. Then he turns. Do you want to honor Christ's body? he asks. Then don't ignore him when he's naked. Don't honor him in here with silk, while outside you pass him by, cold and without clothes. What good is it, he says, if his table is loaded with gold cups, while he himself is dying of hunger? Feed him first when he's hungry. Then adorn his table too. He isn't against beautiful churches. He's against the order being backwards. Where does he get this? From Jesus, in Matthew. At the end of a story about the last judgment, the King says, in the King James words: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Chrysostom takes that at its word. The person at the door isn't only a reminder of Christ. By the words of that Gospel, what's done to him is done to Christ. The same Christ the congregation is about to receive at the altar is sitting outside, asking. Churches understand the altar differently. Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways. All of them can hear Chrysostom's question about the door. The golden mouth didn't keep him safe. His preaching against luxury, the luxury of the powerful included, made him enemies, and he died in exile. His sermons are still read, and that question is still in them: did you see him at the door?

Here's the practice: get ready to see Christ at the door. Settle, and breathe. Recall someone you've passed who was asking: on a corner, at a station, outside a shop. Maybe you gave, maybe you looked away. No verdict either way. Just see their face again, as a face. Then decide one concrete thing for the next time: a coin, a sandwich, a question about their name. If you pray, you can pray for that person, even without a name. If you don't, keep their face in mind for this minute. The bell holds the time.
The golden mouth. John Chrysostom, the preacher who said the Christ honored at the altar is also asking at the door.
Your line: christ at the door. Today, if someone asks you for help, give something, and look them in the eye when you do. Day seven hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: Orthodox and Eastern Catholic churches celebrate the Divine Liturgy that bears John Chrysostom's name, and Christians of different churches honor him as a saint and read his sermons, especially on care for the poor.

original.note: Greek: golden-mouthed. the name people gave John the preacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: a saint with a nice nickname.
what it means: John Chrysostom preached that the Christ honored at the altar is also the hungry person at the door, and feeding him comes first.
what a scholar hears: he roots it in Matthew 25, inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least, and preaches it in a homily on Matthew.

notes: The index hook's wording ('if you can't find Christ in the beggar at the door, you won't find him in the chalice') is a popular paraphrase; the script uses the content of Homily 50 on Matthew (honor Christ's body; silk inside, naked outside; gold cups while he starves; feed him first, then adorn the table). Paraphrased; confirm section numbers.
Nickname Chrysostom = 'golden-mouthed' (Greek). The script says 'people came to call him', without dating it. Confirm.
Biography kept minimal: priest of Antioch, later bishop of Constantinople, made enemies by preaching against luxury, died in exile. Confirm the framing of the cause of his exile.

Eucharist views: 'Orthodox and Catholic Christians speak of Christ truly present in the bread and wine; Protestant churches understand communion in a range of ways.' Note that Lutherans and some Anglicans also affirm real presence; Keeper may prefer different wording.
